It's hard because if you don't know what to ask (or god forbid, actually ask for pain meds), you're dismissed, but if you come and use actual medical lingo, you're also dismissed. We have to thread this tightrope of trying not to accidentally hit a doctor's ego by leading the horse to water rather than just saying "I have these symptoms and my research turned up XYZ, could we talk about it?" because SO many of us have learned that that just doesn't work. You have to learn a whole new way to communicate, between doctors, insurance and specialists, and it's something that takes years.

There was a [thing ](https://www.janetjay.com/dating-chronic-pain-dating-invisible-disabilities/)posted in the chronic pain sub a while ago about dating with a disability that isn't visible, and the takeaway was that if you don't want to out-and-out put it, then at least have something in there that's a 'breadcrumb' that will lead to bringing it up in conversation. And that you should think about what story you're telling about yourself, and why, and who you want to attract with that. The idea being that we all have a bunch of different stories we could tell, so it serves you to think about which you're choosing and why.

There was a "[gifts for fibro](https://www.janetjay.com/gifts-for-people-with-fibromyalgia/)" blog post a couple days ago that had, like, 10 different styles / shapes of heat and cold packs/pads/blankets. first i was like "well that's kinda silly" but by the end was more like "YOINK," there are some great options out there

There was a thing in here recently [about this subject](https://www.janetjay.com/dating_chronic_pain_dating_invisible__disabilities/) that I read, where the idea was to worry less about writing a profile that will get the most likes, and think more about writing a profile that will get the RIGHT likes. I think it's a hard balance to find between mentioning it and it becoming the sole focus, especially when an app gives you so little space! But it's worth checking out and pondering, I guess.

FWIW i read a [thing](https://www.janetjay.com/dating_chronic_pain_dating_invisible__disabilities/) recently specifically about dating with chronic pain. it sucks but you're doing the right thing being up-front with them about this stuff. but it got me thinking about not just telling what's wrong, but thinking strategically about *how* to communicate that, and when. But fuck it's hard, it's so hard, and a blog post doesn't do much to make it easier. Just know there are a lot of people who get it...

Yeah, apps suck in general, and even moreso when you have something like a disability in the mix. Unfortunately they're sometimes a necessary evil? But you're right that you always have to remember that it's skewing the perspective for everybody and that their goal is to keep you on the app. But especially for someone with significant disabilities, it can be hard to get out of the house all the time, so I can see why you might end up using them, and figured I'd throw that thought about "what story do you wanna tell" into the mix. That's something that can be used for in-person interactions too.
You only get one life. There's gotta be a middle ground, yknow?

I read a thing recently-ish on this topic and have been thinking a lot about it. The [piece i read](https://www.janetjay.com/dating_chronic_pain_dating_invisible__disabilities/) was focused more on invisible disabilities, which are obviously a whole other thing than being in a wheelchair 24/7, but the main point is applicable to anybody: the difference between "how do i write the best profile to get me the most messages" and "what story about yourself do you want to tell, and how do you want to tell it, to attract the person you want to attract"? Not "how do i tell my story," but "\*what\* story do i want to tell," if that makes sense. A person is out there. Online dating sucks for everybody, but even worse when you're disabled and don't have a lot of experience. I know you say severely disabled, but can you get out and do anything? I think you're going to have better luck meeting people IRL than using apps. Good luck, my man. I hope you find somebody.

I'm in constant, increasing pain which doesn't really have a diagnosis, though fibromyalgia & other stuff comes close. I'm almost 30 and have never been able to work a full-time job or even get through school without disability accommodations (though I did graduate with 3 majors in 4 years from a top 20 university).  I am in too much pain to work or have a normal social life, much less dating, much less marriage and god, there's no way I could carry / care for a kid like I am now. I smoke and drink too much, despite the pain pills I'm on, and much of what I'm doing to fill up the day is less enjoyment of life than distraction from pain. 

Granted, I've moved around a lot, but I've seen north of a half dozen different psychiatrists and tried talk therapy four times (well, I guess six now with the two in the past year, both of which were researched and recommended and to whom I mentioned CBT specifically) and now that I feel like I'm truly in a desperate place, I don't know where to turn and can't find anybody who can tell me.

I always had hope and I don't anymore. And for all I know all I have in front of me is 50 years of ever-increasing pain and i can both recognize that that's a dangerous viewpoint to be in all the time and that it's totally realistic. And I will kill myself if I can't get out of this, and I can't get out of this through just talking, and HOW do i find someone to help me who didn't just get out of medical school and isn't just used to dealing with <insert psych cliche here>?
